approach_variants.name: Eightmile Lake to Lake Caroline and Windy Pass
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep once the snowfield below Windy Pass has gone; Jun trips normally still find snow on the traverse
approach_variants.notes:
Eightmile Lake Trailhead, reached off Icicle Creek Road and Eightmile Road. Start on the Eightmile Lake Trail (#1552). At about 2.8 miles, just past Little Eightmile Lake, a junction appears — go right onto the Eightmile-Trout Creek Trail (#1554), signed for Lake Caroline.

That trail switchbacks up through a recovering burn. At roughly 5.5 miles it crosses the ridgeline and drops to Lake Caroline, then continues past Little Lake Caroline. From Little Lake Caroline it is about another 0.8 mile toward Windy Pass; Mount Stuart, Dragontail and Colchuck Lake come into view as you gain the pass.

Leave the maintained trail at about 6,850 ft and walk cross-country to the east. Camp spots and the last reliable water appear a little further on, around 7,100 ft. From there climb north-northeast to the broad col on the peak's west side.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The scrambling starts at the broad col on the west side, but the col is not the part people get wrong — the gully is.

Working east from the col you pass a run of tooth-like gendarmes. Do NOT commit to a chimney or gully while you are still among them: stay low, on the SOUTH side while you pass the western spires, then cross onto the north face and keep traversing low rather than climbing.

The gully you want only presents itself once you are on the NORTH side and the END of the summit formation is in sight ahead of you. From there a class 3 gully opens directly above you and leads to a notch. Standing in that notch you can see down the far side of the mountain — that view through is the confirmation. From the notch it is easy scrambling straight up the crest with one short corkscrew move to a summit block no bigger than a dinner table.

Two errors are on record and they are opposite. If the ground is pushing you into fourth-class moves, or the summit formation still runs on ahead of you, you took a gully too early. If you find yourself climbing a cliffy step out of a notch, you walked past the correct gully and are forcing the first notch you came to.
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the class 3-4 ground from the col upward
Rockfall onto your own party — the standard advice is to keep the group tight rather than strung out
A snowfield below Windy Pass that persists into mid-summer; an axe or microspikes are worth carrying
A summit block only about the size of a table, with gusts reported over 30 mph

approach_variants.name: North-side scree traverse to the ridge crest
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; in early season the north side holds steep snow
approach_variants.notes:
Reached from the same Eightmile Lake / Lake Caroline / Windy Pass approach as the West Ridge — Eightmile Lake Trail #1552 for about 2.8 miles to the junction past Little Eightmile Lake, right onto Eightmile-Trout Creek #1554 to Lake Caroline, then on toward Windy Pass and cross-country east onto the west end of the mountain.

Rather than staying on the crest, cross over to the north side of the ridgeline below the summit pyramid and traverse the north-facing scree field eastward.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ridge is joined, not climbed to from a distinct base, so the question is whether you are on the right crest.

You are on the northeast ridge when you have finished crossing the north-facing scree field and are standing on a crest that runs directly up at the summit pyramid, with the north face dropping away steeply behind you. From there the line goes straight up.

If you are still weaving back and forth between notches on a crest studded with gendarmes, you are on the WEST ridge and have not crossed far enough. If you are traversing under the summit rather than up at it, keep going: the ridge is gained at its low point below the pyramid, not partway up the face.

In early season the north side changes the route's character entirely — parties report steep snowfields with poor run-outs, and the alternative of staying on the crest becomes exposed class 3 rather than a scree walk. An easy, dry scree traverse is the summer case only.
hazards: Steep north-facing snow with poor run-outs in early season
Loose scree on the traverse
Exposed class 3 if you stay on the crest instead of traversing

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Trail, old logging road and the burn
approach_variants.season: May-Jun; the southeast aspect and thinner snowpack clear earlier than the Windy Pass side
approach_variants.notes:
Start up the Eightmile Lake Trail. Not far in, leave it and push through brush onto an old logging road — this is scrappy going and there is no sign.

From the road, head up the hillside into the burn. The next thousand feet of gain is booting up ashen slopes and stepping over deadfall in a fire scar young enough that little more than shrubs have come back.

Above the burn the angle eases. Go cross-country up and to the LEFT, aiming at the southeast gullies. A snowfield is normally crossed before the gullies proper; a cold night leaves it firm enough to want crampons even in June.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route takes the gully between the south and southeast ridges, and above the snowfield more than one gully line is on offer.

The correct one is easy: class 2 to 3 on reasonably solid rock. That is the test — the scrambling should stay hands-on but casual the whole way. The recorded error is trending too far LEFT out of the gully, which drops you straight into harder ground; if the difficulty stiffens past easy class 3, you have drifted left and want to work back right into the floor of the gully.

Expect thin ice glazing the rock in the gully even on a June ascent, and note that access to the final scramble can itself be the problem early in the season — carry an axe and crampons if in any doubt.

One honest limitation: in fog there is nothing above the burn to navigate by, and a party who climbed this in cloud reported simply not being able to see enough to distinguish the gullies. This is a poor route to attempt in poor visibility.
hazards: Bushwhacking and deadfall on the old logging road and through the burn
Loose ash, dirt and standing dead trees in the fire scar
A firm snowfield below the gullies early in the season
Thin ice on gully rock even in early summer
Gullies effectively indistinguishable in fog

approach_variants.name: Prusik Pass to the northeast summit
approach_variants.season: Late Jun to early Oct for snow-free ground; outside that the basin travel needs snowshoes or skis
approach_variants.notes:
Prusik Pass is reached either from the west — Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake, Aasgard Pass, then across the core Enchantment basin — or from the north and east on the much longer Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail (#1553) into the upper basin.

From the pass the line heads west and up the peak's shoulder. Most of it is walking with occasional use of hands, class 2, along the eastern arm; there is a single steeper step at around 7,900 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock base to find here — you walk onto the ridge from the pass. What you have to get right is WHICH SUMMIT you finish on, and this is the trap on Enchantment Peak.

The climbing proper is the last fifteen feet or so: a short third-class pull onto a small flat block roughly six feet square. If your top-out was a short, fun scramble onto a table-sized block, you are on the northeast summit — and a 2023 survey put that summit six to seven feet HIGHER than the southwest one, so this is the true high point despite being the easy one.

The negative marker: if you have traversed a long way southwest along the crest and are being drawn into sustained, very exposed fourth-class ground, you have left the northeast summit behind. The southwest summit lies about 1,500 ft further along the crest and is a serious exposed fourth-class scramble, not a continuation of this route.

If you top out on something broad and walkable with no scramble at all, you are on one of the intermediate bumps between the two summits, which are noticeably lower than the northeast top.
hazards: A single steep step on the east arm around 7,900 ft
Snow lingering across the basin approach and the shoulder well into summer
Committing onto the crest toward the southwest summit turns the day into exposed 4th class

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the core basin to the southwest side
approach_variants.season: Late Jun to early Oct snow-free; Apr-Jun normally needs an ice axe for Aasgard Pass and the upper basin
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead on FS Road 7601. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 north through forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on footbridges, moderate for the first 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake junction — go left and uphill. Steeper and rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. That is the last easy water before the high basin.

Skirt the lake's south shore to the foot of Aasgard Pass and climb the pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles on faint tread, cairns, loose talus and boulders.

Aasgard has one route-finding rule that matters more than any other and it has killed people. A few hundred feet above the lake the path veers to the climber's LEFT of the creek. Keep left. At the first grove of larches, stay well clear to the left of the rock, whatever the season. At around 6,400 ft stay LEFT of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it, and do not follow any side path toward the waterfall. Drifting right of the trees, toward the waterfall ground, is how parties get cliffed out.

From the pass drop gently into the upper core basin past Isolation Lake and traverse cross-country on use-paths and cairns through the Tranquil / Perfection / Sigrun / Reginleif tarns toward the Enchantment Peak massif. A common line for the southwest summit leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus onto the peak's south side.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The scrambling starts where the basin talus steepens onto the peak's south flank — there is no cliff base, just a change of angle, so the useful test is about the summit rather than the start.

The southwest summit is reached by a very exposed fourth-class scramble. If what you are on is class 2-3 with a fifteen-foot third-class finish onto a small flat block, you are NOT on the southwest summit — you are on the northeast summit, roughly 1,500 ft away along the crest, which a 2023 survey found to be six or seven feet higher. Those are two different tops and two different days.

On the way in, the marker that you have left the basin at the right place is the pair of lakes: the line goes between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun onto the south side. If you are heading for Prusik Pass you have taken the longer, mellower option, which is a reasonable choice in spring conditions but does not lead to this scramble.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose shifting rock and genuine rockfall risk onto parties below
Getting cliffed out right of the trees / near the waterfall band at ~6,400 ft — fatalities are on record there
Early-season snow and ice turning the pass into a steep exposed snow climb
Sustained exposure on the class 2-3 talus and slab above the basin, worse when snow lingers
Fragile alpine ground in the permit core zone — stay on rock or snow

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes to the core basin, then McClellan Ridge past the Prong
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; late-season the slope below the ridge often goes icy
approach_variants.notes:
Snow Lakes Trailhead on Icicle Road about 4.2 miles from Leavenworth. Snow Lakes Trail #1553 climbs steadily through forest, passing Nada Lake at roughly 4 miles, then Lower and Upper Snow Lakes — the logjam between the two lakes is the known crossing hazard, especially at high water or on a pre-dawn start.

Above the Snow Lakes the tread coarsens into a climbers' path and switchbacks steeply into the core basin past Lake Viviane, then Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes. By this point most of the day's elevation is behind you.

Leave the trail at the flat, open ground around 7,000 ft between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes and head south-southeast for McClellan Ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two features decide this route and both are recorded errors.

First, the Prong: a distinct rock tower standing on the ground above you. The line keeps WEST of it, climbing steep talus, scree or snow to gain the ridge crest. Parties who drift the other way, west into the jumbled cluster of towers called the Chessman, report dead-ending in impassable ground and having to traverse back north to find the correct line.

Second, and this is the one that costs people the summit: once you are on McClellan Ridge, do not start up the first thing above you. Scramble EAST along the SOUTH side of the ridge and keep going around until you are on the SOUTHEAST side of the summit block. From there it is an easy class 3 scramble that needs no thought.

The test is your first move. If it is a tricky slab followed by a chimney, you are on the SOUTHWEST side and have stopped short — a few more minutes around to the southeast turns the same summit into a walk-up. Parties have also gained the crest and had to drop about seventy vertical feet before wrapping round to the south side.

No reliable water past the lakes in the basin, and no water at all on the upper section.
hazards: The logjam crossing between Lower and Upper Snow Lakes, worst at high water or in the dark
Steep snow below the ridge that turns firm and icy in late season — an axe or microspikes are worth carrying
Loose talus and scree gaining the ridge
No water above the basin lakes
Real route-finding with no trail on the upper half

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Creek and Crystal Creek from the south
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
This is the back side of the mountain and has nothing to do with the Enchantments core approach. From Highway 97 south of the Y-junction, drive about 7.5 miles and turn onto Ingalls Creek Road to the trailhead.

The Ingalls Creek Trail is a gentle, well-maintained walk. Pass the Fall Creek trail junction at about 5.5 miles and continue roughly two more miles, to a point around 8 miles in where the Crystal Creek valley opens above you to the north.

Leave the trail on the right (north) at about 3,700 ft and climb moderate slopes, following cairns, into brushy ground up Crystal Creek. About 2,200 ft of gain brings you to a meadow-and-tarn basin near 6,000 ft, the usual camp.

Carry water. Parties have run out and become dehydrated on this approach, and the cairned path is easy to lose — descending parties routinely miss it and end up bushwhacking back to the Ingalls Creek trail.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the tarn the route goes up a large talus-apron gully lying WEST of the tarn, toward a col at roughly 7,700-7,880 ft between Little Annapurna and the spires to its south. The technical climbing is on the south face above that, reached through the gully.

The grade is the check: this face is around 5.5 to 5.6 over three pitches on solid rock. If you are on ground appreciably harder than that, you are not on the line.

The strongest negative marker on this peak is the summit itself. Little Annapurna is reached from the Upper Enchantments by an essentially class 1 walk-up and is often called the easiest Bulger — so if the terrain above you never becomes technical, you have wandered onto the ordinary walking side of the mountain rather than the south face, and the day is a hike, not a climb.

This approach is only weakly documented and no source consulted gives a per-pitch description of where the first pitch begins within the gully system; treat locating the exact first belay as work to be done on the ground.
hazards: No reliable water once you leave Ingalls Creek — dehydration is on record here
Brush and route-finding up Crystal Creek; the cairned path is easily lost, especially on descent
Long walk out from a remote basin

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass to the east saddle
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep for a scramble; the Snow Creek Glacier basin usually holds snow into late July
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft of gain.

From the lake's west side follow the cairned climbers' path up Aasgard Pass, gaining roughly 2,200 ft in about three quarters of a mile.

The pass itself is where people get hurt, and the rule is simple: stay LEFT. A few hundred feet above the lake the path crosses to the climber's left of the creek and stays there. At the first grove of larches keep well clear to the left of the rock, in any season. At about 6,400 ft stay left of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it and ignore every side path leading toward the waterfall — deaths are on record on that side, and the right-hand ground cliffs out.

From the top of the pass head right and south along a short ridge above a tarn to reach Dragontail's east saddle, then cross the Snow Creek Glacier basin — a mellow slope with little crevassing, snow-covered through most of the summer — to the saddle on the east ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route has no rock base; what you are identifying is the saddle, and the confirmation is a change of medium.

You are at the right place when the snow or till of the Snow Creek Glacier basin ends against the crest of the east ridge at a saddle, with the ridge running west up toward the summit ahead of you and the ground on the far side dropping away. From there it is a class 3 scramble and ridge walk with a few airy sections, nothing harder.

If you are still on the pass looking at the tarn, you are short — the short ridge above the tarn only takes you to the east saddle, and the basin crossing comes after it. If the ground you have gained requires roped climbing, you are not on this route: Dragontail's technical lines are all on the north side, reached from Colchuck Lake, not from Aasgard.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose rock, rockfall onto parties below, and cliff-out terrain right of the trees near the waterfall band at ~6,400 ft
Snow in the Snow Creek Glacier basin into late July — firm early in the day
Airy sections of class 3 on the ridge

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, counter-clockwise to the north face talus
approach_variants.season: Apr-Jul; the couloir holds snow and ice into mid-summer
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail then Colchuck Lake Trail about four miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

From the lake go counter-clockwise around to the SOUTH side, then head uphill on talus and snow toward the base of Dragontail's north face, aiming a little EAST of the face's lowest point. The base of the couloir sits at roughly 6,400 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The name is the base-finding instruction, and it is the most useful fact about this route: the first couloir of the Triple Couloirs system is called the HIDDEN Couloir precisely because you cannot see it from Colchuck Lake.

So the test runs backwards from the usual one. If you have picked out an obvious couloir line from lake level and walked at it, you are not looking at the Hidden Couloir — you are looking at something else on the face. It only opens up once you are close under the wall.

What you are aiming for from the talus is the prominent snow finger at the foot of the north face, a little east of the face's lowest point, at about 6,400 ft. The first couloir gives roughly 800 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice — sustained but not technical. The hard parts of the wider route are the transitions between couloirs, not the couloirs themselves, so easy climbing at the bottom is expected and is not a sign you are off line.

If you have ended up at the very lowest point of the wall rather than east of it, you are at the Gerber-Sink start, a different route.
hazards: Overhead rock and icefall on the apron below the north face
Talus and moraine travel around the lake, awkward under snow
Snow and ice at 40-50 degrees for the first 800 ft

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake to the toe of the nordwand
approach_variants.season: Summer as a rock route; late winter and spring for ice and mixed, which is how it is usually climbed now
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft.

In the winter and spring conditions most parties come for, this is a much bigger undertaking than the summer figure suggests: expect snowshoes or skis, real avalanche exposure, and most parties camping at the lake rather than trying it car-to-car. Allow three to five hours from the lake to the base depending on the snowpack.

From the lake, work up talus and snow along the moraine beneath the north face. Move as a rope team across the apron below the wall — the overhead rock and icefall hazard is the reason.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Gerber-Sink takes the LOWEST point of Dragontail's north wall. That is the whole test, and it is a thing you can see rather than a distance you have to pace out.

Standing on the moraine, find the point where the talus and snow apron runs highest into the rock — the toe of the face. Triple Couloirs starts further LEFT (west) of it and Backbone Ridge with its Fin is further RIGHT (east); Gerber-Sink is the line between them, out of the toe. In winter conditions the easiest entry is just to the RIGHT of the toe of the face.

Higher up, the feature that confirms the line is the dome or tower sitting BETWEEN Backbone's Fin and the tower at the foot of the third of the Triple Couloirs — the route traverses across it. If the feature above you is one of those two towers rather than the dome between them, you are on the wrong side of the correct line.

One inverted marker worth knowing: the first 800 ft or so is low-angle simul-climbing before you reach the rock band where the technical climbing starts. Easy ground at the bottom is correct here and is not evidence that you are off route.
hazards: Overhead rock and icefall on the apron below the face — move as a rope team
Avalanche exposure on the winter and spring approach
800 ft of simul-climbing before any belayed pitch
Long approach from the lake under snow (3-5 hours)

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Glacier to Colchuck Col
approach_variants.season: May-Jul, best on a firm consolidated snowpack
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — roughly 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft.

This one does not use Aasgard Pass. Continue around the lake's west and south side toward the Colchuck Glacier under the Colchuck-Dragontail col. Ascend talus and then the glacier: mostly snow early in the season, turning to firmer neve and ice with talus showing through by late season. The east lobe is generally reported free of significant crevassing but gets hard enough to want crampons and an axe. Late in the season a band of blue ice can span most of the snowfield, and parties have found a continuous snow finger on the right to get past it.

Allow three to four hours from the lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Climb the glacier to Colchuck Col. The couloir entrance is NOT at the col — it is a couple of hundred feet LEFT of it, meaning east, toward Dragontail.

The confirmation is what the gully ends in. Pandora's Box is a notch that goes right THROUGH the ridge: standing in it you look down the far side, into the Colchuck basin on one hand and the Dragontail side on the other. If the gully you are in simply fades out onto a summit slope rather than opening into a slot you can see through, you are in the wrong feature.

From the notch the summit is reached by descending a little and traversing left, north-east, toward the top; there is also an exit about thirty feet below the notch leading left onto twenty feet or so of class 4 rock and then the ridgeline.

If you have topped out at the col itself with Colchuck Peak on your right, you have simply reached the col and not yet started the route — walk left along the base of the ridge.
hazards: Firm morning snow and ice on the glacier — crampons and axe
A blue-ice band across the snowfield late in the season
The couloir is a fall-line funnel for rockfall and icefall from above — start early, before sun-loosened debris and softening snow

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to 7,300 ft, then right across scree
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction at 2.6 miles, then on to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft.

From the lake's south side pick up the Aasgard Pass climbers' path and climb roughly 85 percent of the pass, to about 7,250 ft. Keep to the climber's LEFT throughout the pass — at the larch grove and again at the cliff band with the waterfall near 6,400 ft — and do not follow side paths toward the waterfall.

At about 7,250 ft the main path crosses the largest braid of the creek that drains the pass. This is the pass's main water source and can thin out by late summer. Continue five to ten minutes past that crossing, then leave the path somewhere between 7,300 and 7,400 ft and make a rising traverse RIGHT across loose scree toward the toe of Dragontail.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base sits about 300 ft BELOW the point where the top of Aasgard Pass meets the toe of Dragontail — so you are aiming under the junction of pass and mountain, not at it. Overshooting up the pass and then coming down is the common error.

The start is described as being in the middle of the protruding tower. On the ground the marker is above your head rather than at your feet: the first belay ledge is roughly 190 ft up and carries two bushes, and the route starts directly below the RIGHT-HAND side of the right bush.

The first pitch also identifies itself by how it climbs. Fifty feet of easy ground leads to about ten feet of face moves around the RIGHT side of a recessed pod, and then back into the main crack system. If your first fifty feet is hard, or if there is no recessed pod to skirt, you are not on it.

The scree traverse in is the crux hazard of the approach — loose, exposed, and consequential given what is below.
hazards: Loose, unstable scree on the exposed rising traverse to the base
Aasgard Pass rockfall, and cliff-out ground right of the trees near the waterfall band
The creek braid at ~7,250 ft is the only water and can dry up late in the season

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall; the wall is low and faces east, so midsummer bakes
approach_variants.notes:
From the Icicle Road junction at the west end of Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Walk the Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill for roughly two to two and a half miles — about an hour — until the wall stands directly opposite you across the drainage. The trail never touches the rock, so what you are watching for is the wall coming abeam, not a junction or a sign.

At one of the first easy openings, branch right off the trail and scramble down into the flat ground beside Snow Creek to find the log crossing. On the far bank, climb up through boulders and talus until a bootpath forms; it gains about 500 vertical feet to the base of the wall.

Weekends are busy and this is the most popular route in Leavenworth — a queue at the base is normal.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Find the route by its top, not its bottom. Outer Space is the long, well-cleaned crack splitting the upper headwall — the Shield — and it is the most obvious single feature on the wall. Trace that crack downward to where it ends at a ledge with several bushes on it.

The route's own original start is the ledge-and-dihedral system about 80 ft RIGHT of that point and 100 ft DOWN from it.

In practice most parties never use that start: they climb the first pitches of Remorse instead, which begins essentially where the climbers' trail arrives at the wall. That arrival point is the highest part of the wall's base, with a few small scrub trees on it. Standing there, the clean bolted slab straight in front of you is RPM's first pitch at 5.10d; Remorse's much easier line is the often-vegetated gully about 30 ft to the RIGHT of it.

So the single most useful test at the base: if your first move off the ground is a hard, blank, bolted friction slab, you are on RPM, not on the Remorse start to Outer Space. Step right into the scruffy gully.
hazards: The log crossing of Snow Creek — high water in spring
Loose talus on the 500 ft climbers' trail below the wall
East-facing, low-elevation rock that gets very hot in summer
Annual raptor monitoring in this drainage; check for a current nesting closure before going
Crowds and parties above you on the most popular route in the area

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing, then 150 yards left along the base
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall; midsummer is hot on this east-facing wall
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles from the west end of Leavenworth to the Snow Creek trailhead; Northwest Forest Pass to park.

Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill roughly two to two and a half miles, about an hour, until the wall is directly across the drainage. Branch right at an early opening, scramble down to the flat ground by Snow Creek and cross on the log. Up through boulders and talus on the far bank to a bootpath that gains about 500 ft to the base.

From where the trail meets the wall — roughly under the Shield — walk LEFT along the foot of the wall for about 150 yards, until the base and the path start dropping steeply downhill. That drop is the signal to stop. Rack up and stash packs there.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Scramble up and left over easy ground toward a large evergreen sitting below the prominent Mary Jane dihedral, which is the biggest feature overhead here and the thing to navigate on.

The published description of a 'hanging tree with many slings' actively misleads people and is worth knowing about in advance: the tree is not hanging — it is roughly horizontal — and it carries no slings at all. The slings are on the ROCK beside it. Do not stand about looking for a slung tree; you have probably already found the tree.

Use the gully on the LOOKER'S LEFT of that tree for the easiest way up. The last moves onto the ledge are about 5.6 and feel exposed, and some parties rope up for this scrambling.

You are on the right ledge when there is an obvious squeeze chimney directly above you — that is pitch one. If you have scrambled to a ledge and there is no chimney above it, you are on the wrong ledge; and if you are still walking on level ground at the foot of the wall, you have not gone the full 150 yards.
hazards: Exposed 5.6 scrambling on the approach to the first ledge, unroped by most parties
The log crossing of Snow Creek at high water
Loose talus below the wall
Mountain goats habituated to climbers at the base

approach_variants.name: As for Orbit, then one pitch up
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Orbit. Icicle Road 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead, Snow Creek trail about two to two and a half miles until the wall is opposite, right off the trail to the log crossing, then up boulders and talus and a bootpath gaining roughly 500 ft to the base.

From where the trail meets the wall, go left along the base for about 150 yards until the base and path start dropping steeply. Scramble up and left toward the large evergreen below the prominent dihedral, taking the gully on the looker's left of the tree.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route does not start from the ground, and that is the single fact that matters.

Mary Jane Dihedral begins from the nice flat ledge immediately ABOVE the Orbit chimney — climb Orbit's first pitch (the squeeze chimney) and the flat ledge you arrive on is the start. From there the first pitch goes straight up through some vegetation and a small overlap to a bolted hanging belay.

If you are standing on the ground craning up at the dihedral looking for a way onto it, you are one full pitch below the start. The dihedral itself is the most prominent feature above this end of the wall and is the landmark the Orbit approach scramble aims at — being able to see it clearly means you are in the right place, not that you are at the base of the route.
hazards: Exposed 5.6 scrambling to reach the Orbit ledge
A hanging belay at the end of the first pitch
The log crossing of Snow Creek at high water

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead. Follow the trail roughly 1.5 to 2.5 miles until you are in the trees running parallel to the wall and the wall is directly opposite.

A path drops right through the woods to the log crossing on Snow Creek. Cross, then climb boulders and talus on the far side onto the bootpath that gains about 500 ft to the foot of the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Iconoclast starts from the ground, at the HIGH POINT of the wall's base — the same arrival point as RPM and Remorse.

Stand on the trail just to the LEFT of the small scrub trees that mark the highest part of the base. You want to be directly beneath the roofs that form the underside of Two Tree Ledge. The confirmation on the rock is a large flake wrapped in a lot of old slings, sitting about 20 ft below a small bush.

That flake is the marker. If you cannot see a heavily slung flake, or you have walked to where the base is dropping away downhill, you have gone left toward Orbit and too far.

Most parties do not climb Iconoclast's own opening — they use the first two pitches of Remorse or RPM and join it above. If you take that option, the same base test applies: the bolted slab straight ahead of you where the trail arrives is RPM at 5.10d, and Remorse is the easier vegetated gully roughly 30 ft to its right.
hazards: Loose talus on the climbers' trail
The log crossing of Snow Creek at high water
Parties above you on the shared lower pitches

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park. Stay on the trail roughly a mile and a half to two and a half miles, until you are almost past the wall.

A path descends through the woods to the log crossing on Snow Creek. On the far side climb boulders and talus to the bootpath, which gains about 500 ft to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Hyperspace runs up the LEFT side of the Shield, and its position on the wall is defined by its neighbours: it sits between Orbit on the left and Outer Space on the right.

It does not have a distinct independent ground start in common use. The two entries are RPM — a runout, dirty 5.10-plus slab — and, more usually, Remorse. Both begin where the climbers' trail arrives at the wall, at the high point of the base with the small scrub trees.

The base test is therefore the same one that catches everyone here: if your first move off the deck is a hard bolted friction slab, you are on RPM; Remorse is the easier, often vegetated gully about 30 ft to the RIGHT.

Higher up, a landmark confirms you: pitch 4 passes a large fresh rock scar, clearly visible from the belay when you look down.
hazards: The RPM start is a runout 5.10+ slab on dirty rock
Loose talus below the wall and the log crossing at high water
East-facing low-elevation rock, very hot midsummer

approach_variants.name: As for Orbit, to the Silver Tongue slab
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead; the trail two to two and a half miles until the wall is opposite; right off the trail, down to the log crossing, then boulders and talus and a bootpath gaining about 500 ft to the base.

From the base, take the Orbit approach — left along the foot of the wall until the ground starts dropping steeply, then scramble up over fourth-class terrain to a pedestal.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Afterburner sits RIGHT of Orbit and the Mary Jane Dihedral and LEFT of Hyperspace, so it is bracketed by three routes you can identify independently.

The staging point is the Silver Tongue slab, beneath a big pine tree — that tree is the landmark, and it gives shade to gear up in. From there go up and LEFT on class 3 ground to just before another large pine on the ledge, where the first belay is built.

The start itself is unambiguous once you are on the right feature: a slab with a single bolt on it. If you are on a pedestal with no bolt in sight, you have not reached it; if you are looking at a chimney, you have gone left onto Orbit.
hazards: Fourth-class approach scrambling to the pedestal
The log crossing at high water and loose talus below the wall

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, then Iconoclast to Library Ledge
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead, then the trail two to two and a half miles until the wall is opposite, right off the trail to the log crossing, and up boulders, talus and the bootpath — about 500 ft — to the foot of the wall.

Ground access is via Iconoclast, which starts at the high point of the wall's base beside the small scrub trees, directly under the roofs of Two Tree Ledge and marked by a large slung flake about 20 ft below a small bush.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arete is visible from the approach trail, sitting between Hyperspace and Outer Space — so you can identify the route from the ground even though you cannot start it there.

Edge of Space does NOT begin at the base of the wall. It is reached by climbing Iconoclast to Library Ledge, and it functions as a two-pitch finish to Iconoclast or as a bolted alternative to Hyperspace.

The test at the actual start is unmistakable and worth knowing before you commit: getting off Library Ledge to the first bolt is a wild, committing deadpoint or jump. If you are standing somewhere you could simply reach up and clip, you are not at the start of this route.
hazards: A committing dynamic move off Library Ledge to reach the first bolt
Several pitches of Iconoclast must be climbed before the route begins
The log crossing at high water and loose talus below the wall

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles from the west end of Leavenworth to the Snow Creek trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass is required.

Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill about two to two and a half miles — roughly an hour — until the wall is directly across the drainage. The trail never touches the rock, so you are watching for the wall to come abeam.

Branch right at the first easy break, scramble down to the flat ground beside Snow Creek and cross on the log. Climb boulders and talus on the far bank until a bootpath forms, gaining about 500 ft to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
RPM is what you are standing under when the climbers' trail runs out. That is the cleanest base-finding fact on this wall: the path tops out at the highest point of the base, marked by a few small scrub trees, and the slab directly in front of you there is RPM's first pitch — a short, dirty, sparsely bolted 5.10d.

So the test is inverted from the usual one. If your first move looks HARD, you are in the right place. Parties who want to avoid that slab step about 30 ft RIGHT into the often-vegetated gully, which is Remorse at around 5.0, and scramble up to rejoin.

Pitch two is the one to confirm on: a dihedral climbed by jamming and laybacking to a three-foot roof at about 35 metres, then easier ground through a V-slot and an easy offwidth to Two Tree Ledge. That pitch is over 60 metres despite looking compact, so a 70 m rope is the working assumption.

Most parties do not climb RPM to the top — they continue up Outer Space after pitch two.
hazards: A sparsely bolted, dirty 5.10d slab as the very first pitch
A rope-stretching pitch over 60 m — a 70 m rope is assumed
The log crossing at high water and loose talus below the wall

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
approach_variants.notes: Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park. Snow Creek trail uphill roughly two to two and a half miles until the wall is directly opposite, then right off the trail, down to the log crossing on Snow Creek, and up boulders and talus onto the bootpath — about 500 vertical feet to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Identical start to RPM, and the arrival point does the identifying for you: where the climbers' trail runs out at the wall you are at the highest part of the base, beside a few small scrub trees, with RPM's bolted 5.10d slab directly in front of you.

If you would rather not lead that slab, the standard workaround is the often-vegetated gully about 30 ft to the RIGHT, which is Remorse at around 5.0 and lets you scramble up to the same place.

The early exit is a decision made on the route rather than at the base: pitch two's crux is a three-foot roof about 35 metres up, and the escape is taken after that rather than continuing RPM's harder line. So at the base there is nothing different to find — if you are hunting for a separate, easier start on the ground, there is not one.
hazards: The 5.10d bolted slab if you lead the direct start
A long pitch two, over 60 m — carry a 70 m rope
The log crossing at high water and loose talus below the wall

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall; the wall is low and east-facing and bakes in summer
approach_variants.notes:
From the Icicle Road junction at the west end of Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead lot; a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Walk the Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill roughly two to two and a half miles, about an hour, until Snow Creek Wall stands directly opposite you across the drainage. The trail stays in trees and never touches the rock.

Branch right at an early opening, scramble down into the flat ground beside Snow Creek, and cross on the log. On the far bank climb up through boulders and talus until a bootpath forms; it gains about 500 vertical feet to the base of the wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The one fixed reference on this wall is where the climbers' trail arrives: that is the HIGH POINT of the base, marked by a few small scrub trees, directly under the roofs forming the underside of Two Tree Ledge, with a large slung flake about 20 ft below a small bush. RPM's bolted slab is straight ahead of you there and Remorse's easier vegetated gully is about 30 ft to its right. Everything else on the wall is located by walking left or right from that spot — Orbit is about 150 yards left, until the base starts dropping steeply downhill.

Honest gap: none of the sources consulted for this pass documents where White Slabs itself starts relative to that arrival point, so no route-specific base marker is recorded here. Identify it on the ground against a current guidebook rather than assuming it shares the Remorse start.
hazards: The log crossing of Snow Creek at high water
Loose talus on the 500 ft climbers' trail
Annual raptor monitoring in this drainage — check for a nesting closure before going

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons and early or late in the day — the wall faces southwest and takes a lot of sun
approach_variants.notes:
Castle Rock sits right beside US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Around milepost 96.5 there is an oversized dirt pullout on the north side of the highway; the rock is visible from the car.

Two different trails leave this one pullout and they go to different halves of the crag. For Upper Castle take the trail from the UPHILL, western end. It climbs and traverses east onto Logger's Ledge, the wide bench that splits the formation in two. Ten to fifteen minutes puts you on the ledge and the first routes are five to ten minutes further.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Logger's Ledge is the test for every Upper Castle route: they all start FROM the bench, not from the ground. If you are at the foot of the rock with the highway noise still beside you, you are at Lower Castle and one full wall too low — that is the trail from the eastern end of the pullout.

On the ledge, Midway is found by the tower rather than by counting routes. It starts at Jello Tower, the pillar standing off the main wall, and the first pitch takes the corner and chimney on the tower's RIGHT side.

The adjacent feature is worth knowing so you do not confuse them: the wide crack and chimney separating the main wall from Jello Tower on the tower's WEST side is Damnation Crack, a much harder line at 5.9+ that starts hand-size and widens to offwidth and then chimney. If your first moves are strenuous wide climbing, you are on the wrong side of the tower.

Expect the rock to be heavily polished — this is a 1948 Beckey line and one of the most-climbed routes in the canyon, so 5.6 here does not feel like 5.6 elsewhere.
hazards: Heavily polished granite that climbs harder than the grade
Full southwest sun on the upper wall
Parties above you on a crowded classic
Descent is a climbers' trail off the back of the formation down to Logger's Ledge

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Oversized dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout; it climbs and traverses east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
As for Midway: every Upper Castle route starts from Logger's Ledge, so if you are at the base of the rock at road level you are at Lower Castle, one wall too low.

The start is at Jello Tower — the pillar standing proud of the main wall — and the ordinary Midway line takes the corner and chimney on the tower's RIGHT side. The direct variation departs from that same feature rather than from a separate part of the ledge, so the tower is what you are looking for, not a second start.

Negative marker: the wide crack and chimney splitting the main wall from Jello Tower on its WEST side is Damnation Crack at 5.9+, and it climbs hands to offwidth to chimney. Strenuous wide climbing from the first moves means you are on the wrong side of the tower.
hazards: Polished rock
Full southwest sun
Parties above you on the shared Midway terrain

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge, then far right
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout — it climbs east across the formation onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes. Then walk the ledge to its far right end.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Saber begins from the FAR RIGHT end of Logger's Ledge, and the feature that names the spot is a large, low ROOF. The route starts on a left-angling ramp immediately to the RIGHT of that roof.

Follow the ramp up until it reaches the base of a left-facing dihedral. That dihedral is the confirmation — and the rock in it is conspicuously polished, which is itself a marker that you are on the right, heavily-travelled line.

The useful cross-check is Canary, which starts about 100 ft to the LEFT of Saber and also on the right-hand portion of the ledge. If you have walked past a start roughly a hundred feet before this one, you passed Canary and are correctly placed.

Both routes finish on Saber Ledge, which is the reference point for the upper pitches. Note that Saber is a 1950 line rated 5.4 to 5.6 depending on the source, and the polish makes it climb harder than either number suggests — do not treat it as a soft lead.
hazards: Very polished granite on the first pitch
Full southwest sun
Sandbagged for the grade because of the polish

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge, then far right
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout, east onto Logger's Ledge, ten to fifteen minutes. Walk the ledge to its far right end.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same start area as Saber, at the FAR RIGHT end of Logger's Ledge. The landmark is the large low roof, with the left-angling ramp immediately to its RIGHT and a left-facing dihedral at the ramp's top; the polish on that dihedral is the giveaway.

The direct is a harder variation on the same feature rather than a separate ground start, so what you are locating is Saber, and the divergence happens on the pitch.

If you are about 100 ft further left along the ledge you are at Canary, not here.
hazards: Very polished rock
Full southwest sun
Harder than the ordinary Saber line off the same start

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout; it climbs and traverses east onto Logger's Ledge, ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Canary starts from the RIGHT-HAND portion of Logger's Ledge and climbs to the top of Castle Rock in three pitches.

The reliable measure is Saber: Canary starts about 100 ft to the LEFT of it. Saber is identified by the large low roof with a left-angling ramp just to its right, so find the roof, then count back a hundred feet left.

The first pitch is the technical crux — face climbing into a dihedral system leading up to Saber Ledge. If you have arrived on Saber Ledge, you are where the route's famous second pitch begins: an airy step straight off the ledge into instant exposure and a traverse that people find far more unnerving than its grade. That step is the confirmation you are on Canary rather than continuing up Saber.

Upper ground gets slabbier with runouts on easier climbing.
hazards: Serious exposure on the pitch-two traverse off Saber Ledge
Runout slab on the upper pitch
Polished rock and full southwest sun

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail on the WEST side of the parking area; it leads up to Upper Castle Rock and Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Damnation Crack is defined by Jello Tower, so find the tower first — it is the pillar standing off the main wall on the ledge.

The route takes the wide crack and chimney that SEPARATES the main wall from Jello Tower, on the tower's WEST side. Midway is on the tower's other side, the RIGHT, and is an easy corner and chimney; so the two routes bracket the same pillar and the side you are on decides which route you get.

The climbing identifies itself immediately: it starts hand-size, widens to offwidth and then to chimney, and the crux comes in the first thirty feet. If your first thirty feet is easy, you are on Midway, not Damnation. Above the crux the chimney stays runout, so the difficulty does not stay at the bottom.
hazards: Runout chimney climbing above the crux
Strenuous wide crack from the ground with the crux in the first 30 ft
Full southwest sun and polished rock

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout, climbing east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Cat Burglar is one of the group of routes on the RIGHT side of Logger's Ledge, the same section that holds Canary, Saber and Century — so the large low roof marking Saber's ramp is the anchor landmark for this whole end of the bench.

The route identifies itself by an awkward first move: a weird step onto a ramp, which then leads into cracks running up to Saber Ledge. The second pitch goes up and to the right.

If your start is a straightforward walk onto easy cracks with no committing move onto a ramp, you are on a neighbouring line. And if you have finished on Saber Ledge, you are where several of these routes converge — the upper pitch is what separates them, and Cat Burglar's goes up and RIGHT rather than traversing left across the exposure like Canary.
hazards: An awkward, committing move onto the ramp at the very start
Shared belay ground on Saber Ledge with several routes converging
Full southwest sun and polished rock

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout; it climbs east onto Logger's Ledge, ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Century is one of the classic trad lines on the southwest-facing upper wall and lies with Cat Burglar, Canary, Saber, Old Gray Mare and Crack of Doom on the RIGHT side of Logger's Ledge.

The reliable anchor for this end of the bench is the large low roof with the left-angling ramp to its right — that is Saber, at the far right end. Canary is about 100 ft to Saber's left. Work from those two known points rather than trying to count lines.

The general Upper Castle test still applies and catches most people: if you are at the foot of the rock at road level rather than standing on a wide bench halfway up the formation, you took the trail from the eastern end of the pullout and are at Lower Castle.

No source consulted here gives Century's own start marker relative to its immediate neighbours; confirm it on the ground against a guidebook topo rather than assuming a position on the ledge.
hazards: Full southwest sun on the upper wall
Polished granite typical of this crag
Descent is by climbers' trail off the back of the formation down to Logger's Ledge

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout, climbing east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Crack of Doom is on the RIGHT side of Logger's Ledge with the rest of the upper-wall classics — Canary, Saber, Cat Burglar, Century and Old Gray Mare.

Use Saber as the anchor: far right end of the ledge, a large low roof with a left-angling ramp immediately right of it. Canary sits about 100 ft to Saber's left. Locate those, then place this route against a topo.

The standing Upper Castle check: all of these begin from the bench halfway up the formation. If you are at the base of the rock beside the highway you are one wall too low, on Lower Castle, and took the trail from the eastern end of the pullout.

No source consulted gives an independent start marker for this route; identify it against a guidebook on the ledge rather than by guessing from the crack width.
hazards: Full southwest sun
Polished rock
Walk-off descent down the back of the formation to Logger's Ledge

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout; it climbs east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
One of the classic trad lines on the southwest-facing upper wall, on the RIGHT side of Logger's Ledge along with Canary, Saber, Cat Burglar, Century and Crack of Doom.

The anchor landmarks for that end of the bench are Saber — far right, large low roof with a left-angling ramp to its right — and Canary, roughly 100 ft to Saber's left.

The standing check for this whole wall: every route here starts from the bench, not the ground. Being at road level means you are on Lower Castle and took the wrong trail out of the pullout.

No source consulted gives a start marker specific to this route; place it against a guidebook topo from the Saber roof.
hazards: Full southwest sun
Polished granite
Walk-off down the back of the formation to Logger's Ledge

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes:
Castle Rock stands beside US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. There is an oversized dirt pullout on the north side of the highway at around milepost 96.5.

Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout. It climbs and traverses east across the broad bench that splits the formation — Logger's Ledge — and reaches the first routes in five to ten minutes, the ledge itself in ten to fifteen.

There is no water at the crag and no named trail number.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identifying feature for everything in this area is Logger's Ledge: a wide bench running across the middle of the formation, reached by an obvious trail from the west end of the parking area. Upper Castle routes are set up FROM that bench.

If you are at the base of the rock at road level you took the other trail — the one leaving the LOWER, eastern end of the same pullout, about fifty yards downhill — and you are at Lower Castle, a full wall too low.

Descent from anything topping out is a good climbers' trail off the back of the formation, returning to Logger's Ledge, and a trail from the ledge leads back to the parking area.
hazards: Full southwest sun; the formation faces predominantly southwest
Polished granite from very heavy traffic
No water at the crag

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes:
Oversized dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth — the crag is visible from the road.

For the Lower Wall, walk from the LOWER, eastern end of the pullout about fifty yards downhill to pick up the climbers' trail, which then climbs steeply to the base. There is also a short trail from the right of the parking area that leads directly to The Fault.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The first thing to get right is which trail you are on. Two paths leave the same pullout: the one from the UPHILL, western end traverses east onto Logger's Ledge and serves Upper Castle. If your path is climbing away east onto a big bench, you are heading for the wrong half of the crag.

The Fault is the leftmost of the Lower Wall's selected routes as they run west to east — The Fault, then Catapult, The Vertebrae, The Bone — and it is the route the short trail from the right of the parking area leads to directly.

The Lower Wall as a whole is recognised by its ROOFS: this half of the formation is described as identified by many roofs, and it sits directly beneath Logger's Ledge. So if there is a wide bench above you and roofs overhead, you are in the right half; if you are standing on that bench, you have gone one wall too high.

Two pitches from here reach Logger's Ledge, and a trail leads from the ledge back down to the parking area.
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished rock
Highway noise and proximity — the crag is right beside US-2

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. From the LOWER, eastern end of the pullout walk about fifty yards downhill to the climbers' trail, which climbs steeply to the base of the Lower Wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Wrong-trail test first: the path leaving the UPHILL, western end of the pullout traverses east onto Logger's Ledge and belongs to Upper Castle. If you are gaining a wide bench halfway up the formation, you are one wall too high.

On the Lower Wall the selected routes run west to east as The Fault, then Catapult, then The Vertebrae, then The Bone — so Catapult is the second along, immediately east of The Fault, which the short trail from the right of the parking area reaches directly.

The Lower Wall identifies itself by roofs and by sitting directly BELOW Logger's Ledge. Two pitches from the base put you on that ledge, and a trail leads from the ledge back down to the parking area — so if your route tops out onto a big walkable bench rather than the summit, that is correct here.
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and heavily polished rock
Roof features overhead at the base

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day

approach_variants.baseFinding:

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — the crag is closed for peregrine nesting for most of the first half of the year
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth near milepost 96.5.

Take the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot and climb the steep hill to Logger's Ledge. Do not stop there: traverse the ledge EAST and then keep climbing a long, steep hillside above it. Reckon on roughly 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from Logger's Ledge to the rock.

This crag closes annually. Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock are seasonally closed for peregrine falcon nesting from 1 April until roughly 31 July, or until the young fledge or the Forest Service determines nesting will not occur. That is a repeating yearly pattern, not a one-off notice — plan around it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You reach the LEFT side of Midnight Rock first, coming up and right from Logger's Ledge. Midnight is the tall face — around 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging, seamed with parallel-sided cracks — and it faces northwest, so it is in shade through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime is the neighbouring formation and is barely developed; if the wall in front of you has almost nothing on it, you have gone past Midnight.

For ROTC specifically, the crucial fact is that it does NOT start on the ground. It begins from an enormous ledge that cuts across the middle of the CENTRE part of Midnight Rock, and that ledge is reached by first climbing Stevens Pass Motel, The Sting, or Wasp.

So if you are standing on the deck scanning the wall for a splitter to start up, you are a pitch too low. From the ledge, ROTC is the dead-vertical splitter running from fingers through thin hands to perfect hands, taking gear the whole way to two inches. A line that wanders or changes angle is not it — this crack is straight and plumb.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trailhead, back down the road to the driveway
approach_variants.season: Comes into condition early — it is south-facing with almost no shade and bakes in high summer
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Snow Creek trailhead on Icicle Road. Careno Crag is the big formation a few hundred feet above the houses just downstream of the lot.

Walk back down the road roughly 0.1 mile and look for a driveway with a sign to the effect that hikers and climbers enter at their own risk — that driveway is the current access. Follow it to a retaining wall, then pick up a trail rising to the RIGHT toward the crags. A sign marking the boundary onto public land appears shortly after you leave the driveway.

The path keeps climbing past smaller outcrops. Around 30 minutes to the crag. A previously used approach appears to have been lost, so keep to this one, stay on the path, and give the residences a wide berth — the lower part is private ground.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Careno Corners starts immediately to the RIGHT of Bale/Kramar, near the LEFT EDGE of the rock — so you are looking at the left-hand end of the formation, not the middle.

The first pitch identifies itself by what it does rather than what it looks like: a steep crack system that moves RIGHT, then traverses back LEFT to a shared belay underneath a large roof. If your first pitch runs straight up with no traverse and no roof above the belay, you are on a neighbouring line.

The route wanders. Pitch two skirts around that roof through an easy gully with some third-class ground, and the crux is pitch three — an imposing wide corner crack that narrows from offwidth down to hands and fists.

Context that helps rule the route in or out: the biggest face on the crag, in the middle, with prominent dihedrals running up it to a large lone tree, is Regular Route. If that is what is above you, you are too far right.

The crag is laid out on multiple ledge tiers, which makes linkups and unusual pitch combinations common — check which tier you are on before counting pitches.
hazards: Private land on the lower approach — access depends on staying on the path and being respectful
South-facing with little shade; genuinely hot in summer
Ledgy terrain where it is easy to be on the wrong tier
Descent is a scramble down climbers' right from the uppermost ledge system; most routes have bolted rappel belays

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trailhead, back down the road to the driveway
approach_variants.season: Early season — south-facing with little shade and no relief in high summer
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Snow Creek trailhead on Icicle Road; the crag is a few hundred feet above the houses just downstream of the lot.

Walk back along the road about 0.1 mile to a driveway signed to the effect that hikers and climbers enter at their own risk. Follow it to a retaining wall, then take the trail rising to the RIGHT toward the crags; a sign marking the boundary onto public land appears shortly after leaving the driveway. The path continues up past smaller outcrops — about 30 minutes in total.

The lower ground is private. Start near the parking lot and traverse above the residences rather than cutting through them.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Regular Route takes the prominent DIHEDRALS running up the middle of the BIGGEST rock face on the crag, aiming straight at a large lone tree. Those are three independent things you can check from below: biggest face, obvious corner system, single conspicuous tree at the top of the line.

The first-pitch test is the thin crack right at the start — that is the crux of the whole route, and it is protected by BOLTS above the thin section. So a hard, thin opening followed by bolts confirms it; if your first pitch is easy or the corners are clean and moderate from the ground, you are on one of the upper tiers or a neighbouring route.

Everything above the first pitch is easier: clean, enjoyable dihedrals on gear from about half an inch to two inches, with small nuts and TCUs on the last pitch.

If you are at the LEFT edge of the rock rather than in the middle of the big face, you are at Careno Corners and Bale/Kramar.

There is an obvious walk-off after pitch three, though the route carries on for a fourth.
hazards: Private land on the lower approach
South-facing, little shade, hot
A thin crux crack right off the deck on pitch one
Ledge tiers that make it easy to mistake which level you are on

Bale/Kramar sits at the LEFT EDGE of the rock, immediately LEFT of Careno Corners — the two are adjacent and Careno Corners is described by its position relative to this route, so they are best identified as a pair.

The confirmation is which end of the crag you are at. The biggest face, in the middle, with prominent dihedrals running to a large lone tree, is Regular Route; if that is above you, you have walked too far right and need to come back to the left edge.

The crag is tiered with several ledge systems, so check which level you are standing on before counting lines across the face.
